title: The emotional influence of different geometries in virtual spaces: A neurocognitive examination
research_question: To empirically measure and quantify the emotional reactions generated by different architectural space geometries (protrusion, curvature, scale, and proportion) in virtual environments, and to examine the connection between visual perception, human emotions, and architectural space.

participants.description: 112 participants (45 male, 67 female), aged 21-46 years. Mean age for designers (n=12) was 33.8 years (SD=5.72), for non-designers (n=100) was 26.24 years (SD=4.73). Exclusions: ADHD, visual deficits (uncorrected), heart disease, pregnancy, vertigo, claustrophobia.
participants.recruitment: Advertisements published on the web, in social media and by word-of-mouth.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 27 virtual 3D models of architectural spaces, generated using Grasshopper plugin for Rhino and exported to Unity real-time engine. Spaces varied in protrusion (P=0, 4), curvature (C=0, 4), scale (S=1, 3), and proportion (height P(H): low, medium, high, very high; width P(W): narrow, standard, wide, very wide).

measures.instrument: EEG (Emotive Insight system, AF3, AF4, T7, T8, Pz electrodes)

measures.construct: Activity fit ('What kind of an activity fits this space?')
measures.instrument: Self-report (7 positive vs. negative uses via VR controller)

findings.quote: On average, the designer (Ds) group had lower physiological measure results than those of the non-designer group (NDs).

findings.consequent: Fixation duration (FD) for protrusion, curvature, and scale MEVs
findings.test_statistic: F=3.2590; df, 107 (protrusion); F=3.2601; df, 107 (curvature); F=3.9695; df, 107 (scale)
findings.quote: The D group obtained higher results than those of ND, only in their fixation duration (FD) measurements of measurable environmental variables (MEVs) of protrusion (F = 3.2590; df, 107; p < 0.0738), curvature (F = 3.2601; df, 107; p < 0.0738), and scale (F = 3.9695; df, 107; p < 0.0489; see Fig. 5).

findings.antecedent: Participant group (Designers vs. Non-Designers) x MEV
findings.quote: There was no interaction effect between group and any MEV.
both symmetric (protrusion (P) = 0) and non-symmetric (P = 4) showed a significantly higher ßratio among NDs, compared to Ds
Significantly higher ßratio was also found among NDs in curved virtual spaces (VSs) (Curvature (C) = 4) and sharp spaces (C = 0)
in large spaces (scale (S) = 3) and small spaces (S = 1), (F = 6.07521; df, 85; p < 0.0157)
in the different proportions of width (P(W)) or height (P(H)) of VSs (F = 6.24984; df, 86; p < 0.0143).
mean pupillary diameter (PD) was significantly higher in protruded (asymmetric) VSs (P = 4) than in non-protruded (symmetrical) VSs (P = 0)
PD was significantly higher in sharp VSs (C = 0) than in curved spaces (C = 4)
large VSs (S = 3) compared to small spaces (S = 1), (F = 96.903; df, 325; p < 0.0001)

findings.antecedent: Proportion (low height VSs, narrow width VSs)
findings.test_statistic: F=103.171; df, 757 (overall); t=-14.046 (low VSs); t=10.100 (narrow VSs)
findings.quote: PD was significantly larger in low VSs (df, 757; t = -14.046; p < 0.0001), and in narrow VSs (df, 757; t = 10.100; p < 0.0001, see Fig. 7).
significant differences in the criteria of protrusion (P4 > P0, F = 18.287; df, 325, p < 0.0001)

findings.antecedent: Proportion (low height VSs, narrow width VSs)
findings.test_statistic: F=14.752; df, 757 (overall); t=-4.190 (low VSs); t=5.013 (narrow VSs)
findings.quote: among different proportions of VSs (F = 14.752; df, 757; p < 0.0001), in which PD was larger in low VSs (SE = 0.223; t = -4.190; df, 757, p < 0.0002), and in narrow VSS (SE = 0.223; t = 5.013; df, 757; p < 0.0001, see Fig. 8).
A significantly higher FR was found in small VSs (S1 > S3; SE = 0.04175817; z-value 4.018549 Pr(> z) 5.855769e-05).
A significantly higher FR was also evident in low VSs (H1 > H3; SE 0.0393; z.ratio -3.109; p < 0.0101)
in narrow VSs (W1 > W3; SE = 0.0415; z.ratio 7.124; p < 0.0001; see Fig. 9).
Significant difference in FD was found between large and small VSs (S1 > S3; F = 6.6165; df, 754; p < 0.0106)
narrow and wide VSs (W1 > W3; SE = 0.812; df, 754; t.ratio 8.233; p < 0.0001).
participants from both groups stayed significantly longer in large VSs (S3 > S1; F = 6.3602; df, 325; p < 0.0121; see Fig. 10).

findings.consequent: Maximal GSR amplitude (MGSR) and rate of GSR peaks (GSRR)
findings.quote: The measured variable of maximal GSR amplitude (MGSR) and the rate of GSR peaks using a mixed-effect model showed no statistical significance.

findings.consequent: Physiological measures (protrusion, curvature, scale, and proportion)
findings.quote: A multivariate mixed-effects model analysis... showed... a significant difference between the physiological measures of Ds and NDs, with higher values for NDs
MPD was the highest of all of the selected physiological measures in sharp spaces (C = 0) and the lowest of all selected physiological mea-sures in curved spaces (C = 4)

findings.consequent: PD and GSR amplitude (high); FD and Beta ratio (low)
findings.quote: In large VSs (S = 3) PD and GSR amplitude were significantly high, FD and ßratio were significantly low.

findings.consequent: PD and GSR amplitude (low); FD and Beta ratio (high)
findings.quote: In small VSs (S = 1), PD was significantly low, GSR amplitude, FD, and ßratio were significantly high
In narrow spaces, FD was significantly high compared to the other physiological measures
A statistically significant difference was found among the mean ß ratio ranks of the 27 scenes of sensor A3 (Friedman test, p < 0.0114).

findings.consequent: Mean Beta ratio ranks (sensors A4, T7, T8, Pz)
findings.quote: The ß ratio ranks of the 27 scenes in sensors A4, T7, T8, Pz did not differ significantly.
A statistically significant difference was found among the mean ranks of the 27 scenes (PD: Chi² = 1469.208; df, 26; p. Chi² = 0; p < 0.01, see Fig. 14a)
(MPD: Chi² = 799.8781; df, 26; p. Chi² = 0; p < 0.01, see Fig. 14b).
the more curved the shape of space (in both symmetric and asymmetrical VSs), the smaller the pupillary diameter.
the greater the protrusion of a space (in curved VSs), the wider the pupillary diameter.
The larger the simple and symmetric VS, the more positive the response (the limit is unknown)
the smaller the symmetric VS, the more negative the emotional response.

findings.antecedent: Curved, large-scale VS vs. large square VS
findings.quote: A curved, large-scale VS is associated with a more positive emotional response than a large square VS.
Positive interest in curvature in this scale could be explained by the existence of a non-immediate peak shift effect, according to high measures of PIS, LS and GSR.
It makes sense that participants prefer the process of recognizing these particular spaces.
large spaces are suitable for multitudes... but also due to their tendency to attract participants to stay in those spaces longer.

Significantly high measures of PD, PIS and LS percentage provided the size criterion, an empiric validation of not only being more practical... but also as an attraction in itself, possibly positive in case of a large dome.
There exists an inverse relationship between the proportion of the VS and emotional responsivity.
The significantly greatest level of emotional reactivity and discomfort were recorded when participants were presented with proportions of significantly narrow width

findings.consequent: Negative interest (perceived threat in inter-personal space)
findings.quote: Negative interest in narrow width could be explained by a perceived threat in inter-personal space, associated with high measures of FR, a relatively large amount of high physiological measures, and low PIS and LS.
If we wish to design spaces which create a high level of excitement, we may use extreme proportions or scale.
narrow spaces, we have found, are experienced significantly more often as distressing, regardless of expertise or advance familiarity.
Is seems that simplicity was associated with a lower level of arousal.
simplicity is "less interesting".
It is assumed that symmetry is more easily perceived, when it is familiar

findings.antecedent: Low interest + Familiarity + Medium scale square spaces
findings.quote: The combination of a low level of interest and familiarity may produce relaxation, or even indifference (specifically in the case of medium scale square spaces, according to the findings of this research).
in symmetrical spaces, if proportions and scale (as well as other criteria such as temperature, light and color) are not distressing... they may benefit activities of concentration and rest.
In this study, complexity or asymmetry evoked more curiosity.
a relationship between the variables of proportionality (extremely narrow/low or wide/high) and the level of interest (high) was significant.

findings.antecedent: Criteria changes (actual threat, especially narrow proportion) vs. Familiarity/high fluency (zero curvature/protrusion)
findings.quote: Criteria changes associated with actual threat (especially narrow proportion) demonstrated a significantly greater impact than criteria associated with familiarity and high fluency (zero curvature and zero protrusion).

findings.consequent: Reported thoughts/feelings, notions about space uses
findings.quote: earlier results indicated a significant difference between designers (Ds) and non-designers (NDs) related to reported thoughts and feelings toward spaces, and their notions about the possible uses of various types of spaces

Empirical evidence of differences between these groups in their physiological measurements indicates that these are significantly greater among ND group participants, with the exception of FD (designers tend to fixate longer)
A higher FD among experts is supported by a recent study that indicated that individuals with high visual aesthetic sensitivity present slower responses in visual aesthetic sensitivity tasks

findings.consequent: Positive evaluation (for Ds); Physiological reaction (weaker for Ds)
findings.quote: The D group tended to be more positive toward non-conformist shapes, characterized by asymmetry or high ceilings, as they evaluated them higher notwithstanding their significantly weaker physiological reaction, relative to the ND participants.
observant designers tend to recognize, focus and experience interest in their areas of expertise (shapes).
Their lesser degree of physiological reactivity may indicate their "immunity" to space criteria manipula-tions, as more extreme spaces are needed to significantly effect a response
The significantly greater number of responses to narrow proportions relative to the other shapes investigated can be explained on the basis of perceived threat to personal space

findings.consequent: Reactions (similar to negative reactions, longer FD, larger PD)
findings.quote: Measurements taken from participants who are present in narrow/low pro-portions of VS demonstrated similar reactions.

findings.consequent: NOF (number of fixations) and FD change
findings.quote: A change in proportion was associated with NOF and FD change which could indicate either an emotional state, or simply be related to the field of view (process of space perception).

findings.consequent: Change in PD (high measurements correlated with low curvature)
findings.quote: change in curvature was associated with a change in PD (high measurements were correlated with low curvature).
the D group's experience with design was associated with lowered respon-sivity to normally unfamiliar shapes.

mechanisms: The brain responds differentially during aesthetic judgment, even in the absence of behavioral aesthetic rating differences between experts and non-experts in the arts.
The time of presence participants choose to spend in the process of that experience.
The ability to recognize potentially 'harmful shapes' is important to survival.
The visual cortex contains cells that are sensitive to a range of different sizes or scales.
The need for 'the eye' to complete an 'unfinished shape' (peak shift effect) is pleasant.
Attention exists mainly in regions of change (e.g., edges), which are more interesting than homogeneous areas, translating to 'pleasing'.
The peak of the response gradient is shifted away from less favorable stimuli towards values beyond reinforcement.
Brain-mapping recordings can measure engagement, interest, and state of mind (creative inspiration, attention, focus).
Beta activity reflects attentional processes, increasing with mental workload and stress.
More curved shapes lead to smaller pupillary diameter, while greater protrusion leads to wider pupillary diameter.
Positive interest in curvature in large scale could be explained by a non-immediate peak shift effect, according to high measures of PIS, LS and GSR.
Participants prefer the process of recognizing particular spaces.
Large spaces are suitable for multitudes and attract participants to stay longer due to their capacity and inherent attraction.
High measures of PD, PIS, and LS for large spaces provide empirical validation for the size criterion as an attraction.
Negative interest in narrow width could be explained by a perceived threat in inter-personal space, associated with high FR, physiological measures, and low PIS/LS.
Extreme proportions or scale can be used to create a high level of excitement.
Narrow spaces are experienced as distressing, regardless of expertise or familiarity.
Simplicity is associated with lower arousal and is 'less interesting'.
Symmetry is more easily perceived when familiar.
Low interest and familiarity may produce relaxation or indifference, especially in medium scale square spaces.
In symmetrical spaces, non-distressing proportions and scale may benefit concentration and rest.
Complexity or asymmetry evoked more curiosity.
Extreme proportionality (narrow/low or wide/high) is significantly related to high level of interest.
Criteria changes associated with actual threat (especially narrow proportion) demonstrated a significantly greater impact than familiarity and high fluency (zero curvature and protrusion).
Designers and non-designers differ in reported thoughts/feelings and notions about space uses.
Physiological measurements for emotional affect are significantly greater among non-designers, except for fixation duration (designers fixate longer).
Higher fixation duration among experts is supported by individuals with high visual aesthetic sensitivity presenting slower responses.

Designers tend to be more positive toward non-conformist shapes (asymmetry, high ceilings) despite weaker physiological reactions, suggesting 'immunity' to space criteria manipulations requiring more extreme spaces for effect.
Observant designers tend to recognize, focus, and experience interest in their areas of expertise (shapes).
The significantly greater number of responses to narrow proportions can be explained by perceived threat to personal space.
Change in proportion is associated with NOF and FD change, indicating emotional state or field of view.
Change in curvature is associated with change in PD (high measurements correlated with low curvature).
Designers' experience with design is associated with lowered responsivity to normally unfamiliar shapes.
implementation_implications: Implications for residential, education, and rehabilitation settings.
Better understanding of human emotional responses to architectural space can lead to better building design and user utilization.
Designing large spaces can create dramatic effects and a sense of awe, suitable for multitudes and encouraging longer stays.
Extreme proportions or scale can be used to create high excitement.
Symmetrical spaces with non-distressing proportions/scale can benefit concentration and rest.
The study's methods can be applied to design more affectively sympathetic spaces for special needs children, educational structures, geriatric and rehabilitation spaces, and public/living spaces.

tables.description: Analysis of emotional response upon recognition of a VS, summarizing physiological and human-centered measurable variables, and assigning arousal scores and interest polarity.

limitations: Inability to precisely evaluate measures according to their relative contribution to the total variance.
Difficulty in determining the actual contribution of individual physiological measures (e.g., FD and Beta ratio contributing equally).
Negative emotion appears easier to recognize, making it difficult to ascertain if the experience was 'too negative' or if physiology was more 'engaged' in signaling negative emotions.
Negative experience is mainly connected to the absence of openings in VS, suspected to be associated with stress.
The experimental setup's colorful nature prior to the experiment might make negative VSs appear more distressing by comparison.
The possibility that negative emotion is simply more strongly expressed physiologically is probable.
Findings relate to a limited parametric change in form and specific orientation of participants towards VSs (e.g., stronger protrusion perceived as threat).
Impossibility of attaching a single measurement to a specific emotional state, necessitating multiple sensors.
